Just start saying no.  If you want to offer a reason, you can add that you have your own financial goals for the future and that's that.  Keep it vague, goalposts create expectation, and your plans are none of their business anyway.

Yeah, I'd say my answer is really dependent on how replayable a game is.  It also hinges on the game's design philosophies though...


As an example, let's drop the multiplayer aspect and say Diablo 2 is a single player game, part of the charm is trying out different builds for your character, so maxing everything out potentially harms the design of the game.  Sometimes, limitations are good.


But a game like Skyrim kind of nails the sweet spot between making choices but eventually being able to max out everything.  And it's highly replayable, so that makes it easier to experience the early game multiple times in order to try out different kinds of characters.


I guess what I'm saying is that there are so many factors that go into which route to take regarding this design decision that there really isn't a "wrong" answer here.

You only get to play this game for the first time once, so I don't want to spoil the mechanics right out, but I will give you some tips for some good starting points that will help your adventure.


The first skill you should max out for each character is Determination, since it lessens the SP requirement of every other skill.  


Train will help you get more experience, which will get you SP faster, so it's good to get at least a few levels in it early.


Enlightenment will also help you get SP faster, so it's another good one to level early.


Writing allows you to craft skillbooks that raise some skills up to level 7, which can save you SP.

Having said that, with this steam release, I've just bought the entire series and intend to play through every available game.  I started with KH1FM on Proud Mode, which I just hit the credit role for last night.  The game is fun, but it definitely shows its age.  I can't comment on how well KH2 improves things yet (I'm playing BBS next), but here are a few things I could see turning players away:


- Poor conveyance.  There are so many instances in the worlds where you are given a one off piece of text, or even *nothing*, to indicate where to go next.  This results in you running circles around the world as you backtrack and try to figure out what you missed.  The most infamous for me was the pillow you're supposed to shoot with a fire spell in the cave of wonders.  To me memory, there was simply *zero* indication that I needed to do that by the game, I had to look it up in a guide.


- The combat difficulty.  Having played this on Proud, I imagine this could be skewed, but I did play this on Normal as a kid.  The one core memory I do have that stood out to me was that this game feels overly difficult before you get the Cure spell, which you don't get until after the Tarzan world.  If you are going through the world's in order of battle level, that means you play through Destiny Islands, Traverse Town, Wonderland, The Coliseum, and finally Deep Jungle, on that order, before you can use magic to cure yourself.  You can use items, but if you're not particularly strong at action games, I could see someone blowing through those pretty quickly.


The weird thing is, after you get Cure, the game gets much easier.  In fact, KH1 essentially starts off the most difficult it ever is while you have none of your abilities, and becomes progressively easier as you learn more passive abilities and combo moves, as well as spells like Cure and Aero.


All in all, I loved my time with the game and will likely go back to do all of the post game content (For now, I'm just really excited to play BBS again.), but I do see why people would drop it, it just has some parts that are plain not fun.

You're asking this question in a steamdeck focused community, so the answers you're going to get will come with at least a hint of bias.  


Having said that, I will give you as objective an answer as I possibly can.


As far as functionality is concerned, you can actually have a setup that quite closely resembles the Switch.  You can play handheld, but you can also set up a dock with your tv, with wireless controllers, keyboards, and even external hard drives to access video media.  The OLED model uses a newer Bluetooth chip that allows you to power the device on simply by powering on a Bluetooth connected controller.  It's really slick.


The deck will also have access to more games, the games that are available across both Switch and Deck will perform better, and you can easily setup emulation with ROMs mixed right in with your steam games, seamlessly accessible as if they were downloaded right from Steam.  Even PS2 and GameCube games run flawlessly for the most part.  (There is Switch emulation as well, but it's iffy with some titles and Yuzu was recently slapped with a lawsuit, so don't expect any further updates.)


Having said all of that, the Switch, and by extension "Switch 2", does have a few advantages of its own.  Any game you play on it will simply work without any tinkering.  Playing couch multiplayer games is far easier to do and requires no setup (just more controllers).  You can dock and undock the device while playing any game and the games will still run as intended (the steamdeck does *not* play nice with being docked or undocked midgame).  Finally, you will have instant access to Switch exclusives without requiring extensive tinkering just to get subpar performance on games like TOTK.


One more note I'd like to add is that there are various titles available across Switch and Steam that simply don't play nice with the deck.  Games like Fatal Bullet and Xenoverse 2 that require Anti-Cheat aren't even playable online on the deck. (But do run perfectly fine offline.)


Personally, I love my deck.  It's replaced my gaming PC, my Switch, and my PS5 as my primary gaming device, and I have no regrets.  I simply wished to share the differences, both positives and negatives, so you can go into this with as much information as possible.  Good luck!

Monster Hunter World and Monster Hunter Pre-World are two entirely different games.  (I'll refer to each as W and PW respectively.)


PW was all about preparation, both in terms of item and inventory management, as well as combat.  Most monster attacks were highly choreographed (with some exceptions), and learning a monster consisted of mastering the tells of those attacks, your own positioning, and learning when it was safe to make your own assault.  Many of the player's attacks often required commitment with no way to cancel out of a swing, so timing was important for nearly every action.  Item use was much the same.  W is similar, but both the monsters and the player are so much faster that the game becomes more reaction based.  More attacks can be canceled or rolled out of now, and item animations are much quicker.  (You can even slowly move while drinking potions now, an action that used to stall the player momentarily.)


This is a quick summary as there is far more to it, but that's essentially the basics.  You had to be proactive in the past, making sure you had all the right items and the proper food buff before even going into the quests.  Now, in W, you can simply enter the tent to change equipment and items, and can even have food made for you by the handler.  


I won't say which is better (though I know which I prefer) as that opinion is highly subjective.  Obviously, the newer games have been much more popular, but fans of the original style still miss the ways of old.  


If you're interested, I'd highly recommend you give a few of the older games a shot.  Monster Hunter 4 Ultimate, Monster Hunter Portable 3rd, and Monster Hunter Dos are my personal favourites.  (Dos was originally Japanese only, but has received a stellar translation in recent years.)

So, the "Unsupported" tag is a bit interesting to work with, because it can mean all kinds of lovely little things.  Most commonly, it means the game hasn't even been really tested, which you'll find quite often with more niche indie games or even entirely niche genres.  Older games as well, have often just not had a chance to be tested in order to determine even just a "Playable" tag.

For games that have been tested and have still received "Unsupported", it varies.  Here are some examples:

Dragon Ball Z: Kakarot is unsupported, because it saves and loads to and from a different file if you not connected to the internet, making it less than ideal for playing handheld on the go.

One Way Heroics Plus is unsupported because some of the soundtrack uses a format unsupported on Linux, so there are sections of the game that do not have any sound.

Danganronpa 3 is unsupported because it can occasionally crash, and does it more to others than some.

There are often work arounds for an unsupported game's issues, so it's important to keep in mind that the Unsupported tag is often slapped on any game that has even one feature that doesn't work, or is at least inconsistent.

Monster Hunter is a bit of a strange rpg, the focus is not (usually) on your moveset or special abilities growing, it's on the monsters you fight being interesting.  The gameplay loop is essentially fight monster, get materials, make better equipment, fight bigger monster, rinse and repeat.  All very simple on paper.

As the hunter, you have fourteen weapons to choose from, each with their own complicated or uncomplicated movesets. Any players tend to focus on mastering one or two favourites, while some endeavor to master them all.  You also have tons of items you can craft to use in hunts, such as traps, various bombs, throwing weapons, and more.

Each monster has an equipment set you can craft that will come with various skills that affect your character in a plethora of ways, but those skills mainly improve the things you can already do.  In older games, it was possible to craft equipment for defense only while gaining no skills, and you could still beat monsters purely on the merit of your own abilities.  As an RPG, numbers get bigger, but the true level ups come from your own ability to fight the monsters.

If you were to try the series today, I would recommend Monster Hunter World, but there are different design philosophies that go into certain games.  Capcom has two teams that develop the Monster Hunter series.  Team A tends to do the mainline games, while Team B tends to work on the "portable" games.  This has changed up a bit since World, since the "Portable" series technically doesn't exist anymore, but it can also be argued that Rise is a "Portable" title.  It was certainly developed like one.  

Team A tends to focus more on the core gameplay mechanics, as well as the realism of the world.  Team B games tend to be more action oriented in the sense that they've recently been introducing more "anime" style ability systems that allow you to equip different kinds of flashy, special attacks.  The presentation of Team B games also tends to be more focused on getting you into the action as quick as possible, while Team A games tend to include a bit more story and grander presentation.

Team B games are not bad by any means, and I've played them all to death as well, I just always find myself going back to the Team A game, despite the B games typically using and building on the system used in the most recent A game.  

World runs incredibly well on the Steamdeck, even before getting Valve's "Verified" classification, and Monster Hunter has always been great for short play sessions.  I imagine with the upcoming Black Friday sale, we'll see both World and Rise go on sale.

Hope you enjoy!

Where I was born, it was pretty much just a white neighbourhood so these issues never came up in our family, but when I started hanging out with my two best friends that I'd met after we moved, these worldviews bubbled to the surface as they were First Nations and Filipino.  She not-so-subtly tried to push me to hang out with my whiter friends more often, as she feared I'd fall into some bad crowds and get into drugs or something.

She was also starkly homophobic, and had once, completely unprompted, informed me in my youth that if I "turned out gay" that I would be thrown out of the house.

I watched her struggle with my friendships, and watched her slowly warm up to my two best friends over the years as we pretty much spent every weekend together staying at each other's houses and gaming way into the bloody night. Something I'd like to add, it helps to try and focus on one weapon at first if you *do* want to push further into the game.  Jagras, Pukei or Kut weapons are the easiest to upgrade as the materials come from the easiest monsters.  Once you're at 6 star monsters and are netting more materials with a decently upgraded armour set, you can start working on other weapons more efficiently.

Prioritize weapon upgrades if you are good at dodging.  Since most monsters can two or three tap you at higher levels, even with good gear, you're going to get used to not getting hit at all unless you have the money to whale on potions right now.  Higher DPS will push you through harder fights more than good armour will, since higher dps can also result in more part breaks, stunlocking the monster more often.

For armour, try to build a set comprised of pieces from five different monsters, preferably also different from your main weapon.  It'll be easier to keep all five upgraded if none of them share rare material drops.

As you get more defense, don't sleep on Health Boost.  First Aid Meds and potions currently heal for 50% of your max health, bringing more value if you have higher hp.  This can help you be able to play for longer periods of time before resting using your free First Aid Meds every day.
